title: The Taped Knuckle
passages:
"No," Kass said, into the set, and loud enough that the open channel carried it up the ore line to Anza's board and out onto the morning desk's relief overflow, where it would sit in a log until somebody with a clean record read it. "Nobody signs anything. Not on my channel."

"Dispatcher," Marlowe said. His voice came through the pump bulb — the old brass horn bolted above the door, spliced into the set at some point before either of them was born — thin but clear, with a splinted man's careful breathing behind it. "You clear loads. You don't clear me."

"It's a trade, not a load."

"It's my body, and I outrank you on it. Desk can requisition cargo. Nobody requisitions a man's ribs but the man." A pause, a wet cough, then: "Kass. Sign it. I've had worse Tuesdays."

Under his voice, faint, a squeak of rubber on a hand pump, in and out, patient as a metronome. Then Rhea, close to the bulb, none of the patience in her voice at all.

"Kass. Take the deal."

"Rhea—"

"Four restarts left. Four. After that I'm squeezing the bag with my hands for however long it takes you to walk back up that grade, and my arm is already gone from the shoulder down." Inhale, squeak, exhale. "I don't want Voss. I want what's on that puck. A reseal carries a time. Get me the time off the sender, get me the six cases, put the scrubbers on a rig. That's all I'm asking."

"The time tells us who shut it," Kass said. "Not whether Voss tells the truth about the rest."

"Nobody's feeding anything," Voss said, from the bench. He had the flat, unbothered look of a man who'd erased himself so thoroughly that weather had more claim on him than people did. "You've got twenty minutes of daylight and a reclaimer with a clearance that turns before eight. Sign, and the scrubbers are yours by seven."

Kass looked at the stack. Eleven cases, Anza's marks on every one, corded and pucked, sitting on a dead pump station's floor like they'd been raised there.

"I want to look at one."

"Nothing in here is free," Brill said. She had her lamp in one hand, a kerosene thing with a cracked chimney, and she held it the way other people hold a wrench. "Not even the light."

"Ospina," Kass said. "What does your ring buy in this room?"

Ospina had been standing with their coat still on, the dirty mark on their authority sitting there like a stain nobody could see but everybody could price. They put their hand out flat. "A receiving counter. Her stock reads Bay 4 sent and Culvert Nine received, in her own ledger, in her own hall. It stops being stolen."

Brill's chin came up. "It also puts my station's name in a ledger."

"Your winter's already got a name on it," Kass said. "Eleven seals off Anza's down-line. Only question left is whether the name is thief or receiver, and that gets decided at eight either way."

Brill set the lamp on the bench and stepped back, which in that room was a signature.

Ospina lifted the nearest case enough to turn it. The sender puck was a steel disk the size of a thumbnail, crimped over the seal wire on the lid: the only thing on a rig that says who shut it and when. Its face is a shallow strike, meant to be read flat under a powered reader, and the pump station had no power, so there was nothing to do but tilt it into the flame and let the light rake across the metal.

"Talk while they look," Marlowe said, over the bulb.

"Quiet," Kass said. "Ospina. Whose?"

Ospina turned the puck a quarter inch. The strike came up out of the steel in pieces, bright where the metal was cut and dark where it was pressed, and Ospina looked at it for a long enough time that the pump bulb hissed and Rhea's hand went around again at the far end.

Behind them, Miko put one hand flat on the overlap log and kept it there.

"Kass," Ospina said. "Hold the trade."

Ospina did not tilt the puck into the flame. They turned the case and held the lid where the lamp's light ran flat along the crimp — the metal ferrule squeezed over the seal wire where the lid's two ears meet, the one part of a case you can't get past without cutting.

"Talk," Kass said.

"Bay 4 Shift 2 on the strike. All eleven, I'd put my ring on it." Ospina's thumbnail went along the crimp and stopped. "Crimp's chipped. There's a notch out of the shoulder, about so." They held up a fingertip. "A die stamps the strike and squeezes the wire in the same pull, so whatever's wrong with the face is wrong with the shoulder too. This die's got a piece out of it."

"File it," Kass said.

"Then the notch moves and the old ones stay put. You can't file a die and un-file it." Ospina set the case down. "I've pulled Bay 4 crimps for nine years. Voss's is square. Square shoulder, every time, like a stamp on a ration card."

"That's mine," Voss said. "Never filed a day in my life." He didn't get up. He took a brass die out of his coat and set it on the bench without looking at it, a man putting down a cup. The face was a square with a flat bar across it, the edges still sharp.

Ospina reached into their own coat and set a second die beside it. Steel, the strike face cut as a crescent with a bar across the belly, and a bite out of the lower horn the size of a thumbnail.

Nobody said anything. The pump bulb hissed.

Ospina picked up the crescent and laid the bitten horn against the notch in the crimp. It seated like a key.

"All eleven," Ospina said.

"Say the rest," Kass said.

"It's been in my coat since Kettering. I found it in the tool void on a northbound med rig the night of the twenty-first." They didn't look at Miko. "Bay 4's. I'm Bay 4 seal authority. I know what comes out of that shop." Ospina sat the crescent on the bench between the two brass-and-steel. "Two dies sealed Anza's eleven. One of them's been riding around in an Anza coat for two days."

"Not mine," Voss said.

"Nobody said it was yours," Kass said. "We said it was in the room."

Voss got up off the bench. It was the first time he'd stood since they came in, and he came as far as the lamp and stopped, looking at the crescent the way a man looks at his own name on a board he thought he'd wiped.

"Where did you get that."

"You heard the lady's coat," Ospina said. "Tool void. Bay 4."

"There's one crescent die on the Interior," Voss said. "It's been in a drawer at the Kettering morning desk since before I could stamp. Whoever had it in that void walked past me twice that night and I never turned around." His voice had lost the flatness. It had edges now. "Who else was in there with it."

The pump bulb hissed. At Anza, rubber squeaked on a hand pump, in and out.

"Later," Ospina said.

"Now."

"You want it on Kass's open channel? Half the relief overflow's listening, and the rest gets it at eight."

Rhea's voice came through the bulb, close and flat. "Kass. The receiving mark. Whose is it, because it isn't any of ours, and I want to know who Anza's been feeding."

Kass reached across Ospina for the case.

Behind them, Miko took her hand off the overlap log, one finger at a time, and put it in her coat pocket.

Kass turned the case so the puck faced the horn and keyed the set off the tight line to Anza and onto the wide one — the whole ore line, the relief overflow, every desk that would be reading a log at eight and pretending it hadn't.

"You want to know who walked past you in that void," Kass said to Voss. "The man in the box saw him. Marlowe. Say it again, slow, for the room."

The pump bulb carried the breathing first, and under it Rhea's hand pump, still squeaking, still patient, still four. Then Marlowe.

"Two of them at the lid," he said. "One had the stamp — square shoulder, I felt it bite the wire over my chest. The other had tape wound up his right knuckles to the second joint, gray gone black at the edges. Clean voice. Like it didn't cost him anything." A breath. "He held the lid down and counted me under it, out loud, the way you count a load you're not scared of. *Twenty-nine. Thirty.* Then the light went out."

The bulb hissed. Nobody in the pump hall moved.

"You heard him," Kass said. "Tape on the right hand, clean voice. You're the stamp, Voss. So who's the count?"

For a breath Voss looked like he'd go back to being weather. Then he reached across the bench, past his square die and Ospina's crescent, and turned the puck up into the lamplight himself, the way a man shows a wound he's decided to own.

"Eleven cases off Anza's down-line," he said. "I resealed them at 05:52. Bay 4, Shift 2, my mark on every strike. At 21:47 I sealed the loader in as ballast — databus already cut, so the box would read warm the whole way north — and I signed the pod out myself. Ballast. That's mine. All of it's mine." The flatness had a seam in it now. "I'm not putting any of it on the other one."

"Kass." Teodoro, from Anza, fast and helpful, the way he was about things nobody had asked him. "Give it back to me. Times. Clean, for the board log."

"Teodoro—"

"The drawer's open. *Twenty-one forty-seven, sealed the loader in as ballast.* Go on. *Oh-five fifty-two, resealed eleven.* And the sign-out — what did you sign the pod out as?"

"Ballast," Voss said, to the puck.

"Ballast," Teodoro said, and read the whole of it back into the set once, slow, every word going down into the drawer at Anza that keeps what it's told. Then he read it a second time — because the first time a man says a thing it can still be weather, and the second time it's a record, and a record is the one thing on the Interior you can't rub out with a chipped crescent or a clean morning.

Kass watched Voss hear it go.

He had wiped himself off the Kettering board so clean that morning the desk had nothing left to read — no strike, no flag, no name but the one he'd walked in here to sell. One clean morning. That was the whole of what the erasing had bought him.

And he'd just spent it out loud, on an open channel, to a room full of relief desks, to find out who held the lid.

"*Ah*," Voss said, very quietly, and sat back down.
